title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
description:
You are given an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is the price of a given stock on day `i`.

You want to maximize your profit by choosing a single day to buy one stock and choosing a different day in the future to sell that stock. Return the maximum profit you can achieve from this transaction. If you cannot achieve any profit, return `0`.
hints: Track the minimum price seen so far as you scan left to right.
At each day, the best profit if you sold today is price[i] - minSoFar. Keep a running maximum of that.

title: Contains Duplicate
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if any value appears at least twice in the array, and return `false` if every element is distinct.
hints: A set only keeps unique values — how does its size compare to the array's length when there are duplicates?
Insert each number into a hash set; if it's already present, you've found your duplicate.

title: Product of Array Except Self
description:
Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `answer` such that `answer[i]` is equal to the product of all the elements of `nums` except `nums[i]`.

You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time without using the division operation.
hints: For each index, the answer is (product of everything to its left) times (product of everything to its right).
Build a prefix-product pass left to right, then fold in a running suffix product right to left.

title: Maximum Subarray
description: Given an integer array `nums`, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) which has the largest sum, and return its sum.
hints: If the running sum ever drops below zero, it can only hurt any subarray extended from it — reset it.
This is Kadane's algorithm: keep a running sum, resetting to the current element whenever the running sum goes negative, and track the best sum seen.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
description: Given an integer array `nums`, find a contiguous non-empty subarray within the array that has the largest product, and return the product.
hints: A negative number can flip the smallest product into the largest — track both a running max and a running min.
At each element, the new max is the largest of: the element alone, max*element, or min*element (and symmetrically for the new min).

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
description: Suppose an array of length `n` sorted in ascending order is rotated between `1` and `n` times. Given the rotated sorted array `nums` of unique elements, return the minimum element of this array. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(log n) time.
constraints: All the integers of nums are unique.
hints: Compare the middle element with the rightmost element to decide which half is guaranteed unrotated.
If nums[mid] > nums[right], the minimum lies to the right of mid; otherwise it's at mid or to its left.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
description: There is an integer array `nums` sorted in ascending order (with distinct values), possibly rotated at an unknown pivot. Given the array `nums` after the rotation and an integer `target`, return the index of `target` if it is in `nums`, or `-1` if it is not. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.
constraints: All values of nums are unique.
hints: At any midpoint, at least one of the two halves is guaranteed to be normally sorted — figure out which.
If the target lies within the sorted half's range, binary search there; otherwise recurse into the other half.

title: 3Sum
description:
Given an integer array `nums`, return all the triplets `[nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]]` such that `i != j`, `i != k`, and `j != k`, and `nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0`.

The solution set must not contain duplicate triplets. Each triplet should be reported with its values sorted in ascending order.
hints: Sort the array first — then fixing one number turns the rest into a Two Sum problem on a sorted range.
For each fixed first element, use two pointers moving inward from both ends of the remaining sorted subarray, skipping duplicate values to avoid repeated triplets.

title: Container With Most Water
description: You are given an integer array `height` of length `n`. There are `n` vertical lines drawn such that the two endpoints of the `i`-th line are `(i, 0)` and `(i, height[i])`. Find two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container that holds the most water. Return the maximum amount of water a container can store.
hints: Start with the widest possible container: pointers at both ends of the array.
The area is limited by the shorter line — moving the taller pointer inward can never help, so always move the shorter one.

title: Move Zeroes
description: Given an integer array `nums`, move all `0`'s to the end of it while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements. Return the resulting array.
hints: Use a slow pointer marking where the next non-zero element should go.
Walk through the array once, and whenever you see a non-zero value, place it at the slow pointer and advance it; fill the rest with zeroes at the end.

title: Majority Element
description: Given an array `nums` of size `n`, return the majority element — the element that appears more than `⌊n / 2⌋` times. You may assume the majority element always exists in the array.
hints: Since the majority element appears more than half the time, a running 'candidate + count' can never fully cancel it out.
This is Boyer-Moore voting: increment a count when you see the candidate, decrement otherwise, and swap candidates when the count hits zero.

title: Missing Number
description: Given an array `nums` containing `n` distinct numbers in the range `[0, n]`, return the only number in the range that is missing from the array.
hints: The sum of 0..n has a simple closed form — compare it against the actual sum of the array.
missing = expectedSum(0..n) - actualSum(nums).

title: Single Number
description: Given a non-empty array of integers `nums`, every element appears twice except for one. Find that single one. Your algorithm must run in linear time and use only constant extra space.
constraints: Every element appears twice except for one.
hints: XOR-ing a number with itself gives 0, and XOR-ing with 0 leaves a number unchanged.
XOR every element together — all the pairs cancel out, leaving only the single number.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays
description: Given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, return an array of their unique intersection (each element appears at most once, order does not matter).
hints: Turn both arrays into sets first — duplicates within a single array don't matter for this problem.
The answer is just the set intersection: values present in both sets.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
description: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k` most frequent elements. If two elements have the same frequency, the one with the smaller value should be placed first. The answer must be returned in that exact order.
constraints: k is in the range [1, number of distinct elements].
hints: Count the frequency of every element with a hash map first.
Sort the distinct elements by frequency descending, breaking ties by value ascending, then take the first k.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
description: Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `k`, return the total number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals `k`.
hints: Track the running prefix sum as you scan the array.
A subarray ending at i sums to k exactly when some earlier prefix sum equals (currentPrefixSum - k) — count prefix sums in a hash map as you go.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
description: Given an unsorted array of integers `nums`, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time.
hints: Put every number in a hash set first for O(1) lookups.
Only start counting a sequence from a number that has no predecessor (num - 1) in the set — that guarantees each sequence is counted exactly once.

title: Rotate Array
description: Given an integer array `nums`, rotate the array to the right by `k` steps, where `k` is non-negative. Return the rotated array.
hints: Rotating by k is the same as rotating by k mod n — handle k larger than the array length first.
The last k elements move to the front, and the first n-k elements shift to the back, keeping their relative order.

title: Plus One
description: You are given a large integer represented as an integer array `digits`, where each `digits[i]` is the `i`-th digit of the integer, in order from most significant to least significant. Increment the large integer by one and return the resulting array of digits.
constraints: digits does not contain leading zeros (except the number 0 itself).
hints: Add 1 to the last digit and propagate the carry leftward, same as elementary-school addition.
If every digit was a 9, the carry propagates all the way past the front — you'll need one extra leading digit (1) in that case.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
description: Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, remove the duplicates in-place such that each unique element appears only once, preserving relative order. Return the resulting array of unique elements.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.
hints: Since the array is sorted, duplicates always sit next to each other.
Keep a pointer to the last unique value written; whenever the current element differs from it, append the current element.

title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays
description: Given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2` sorted in non-decreasing order, merge them into a single array sorted in non-decreasing order and return it.
hints: Use two pointers, one for each array, always taking the smaller of the two current elements.
Once one array is exhausted, append the remainder of the other array as-is — it's already sorted.

title: Pascal's Triangle
description: Given an integer `numRows`, return the first `numRows` of Pascal's triangle, where each number is the sum of the two numbers directly above it (the edges of every row are `1`).
hints: Every row starts and ends with 1.
Each interior value in a row is the sum of the two values above it in the previous row.

title: Sort Colors
description: Given an array `nums` with `n` objects colored red, white, or blue, represented by the integers `0`, `1`, and `2`, sort them in-place so that objects of the same color are adjacent, in the order red, white, blue. Return the sorted array. You must solve this without using a library sort function.
hints: This is the Dutch National Flag problem — three pointers partition the array into 0s, 1s, and 2s in one pass.
Keep low/mid/high pointers: swap 0s to the front (advance low and mid), leave 1s in place (advance mid), and swap 2s to the back (advance high, don't advance mid yet).

title: Gas Station
description: There are `n` gas stations along a circular route. You have a car with an unlimited gas tank. It costs `cost[i]` of gas to travel from station `i` to station `i+1`, and you begin the trip with an empty tank at some station. Given integer arrays `gas` and `cost`, return the starting gas station's index if you can travel around the circuit once in the clockwise direction, otherwise return `-1`. It is guaranteed that if a solution exists, it is unique.
hints: If the total gas is less than the total cost, no starting point can work at all.
Walk through once tracking a running tank total; whenever it goes negative, none of the stations you just passed can be the start, so reset the candidate start to the next station.

title: Valid Anagram
description: Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if `t` is an anagram of `s`, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Two strings are anagrams exactly when they have the same character counts.
Count the frequency of each character in both strings (or sort both) and compare.

title: Valid Palindrome
description: A phrase is a palindrome if, after converting all uppercase letters into lowercase letters and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, it reads the same forward and backward. Given a string `s`, return `true` if it is a palindrome, or `false` otherwise.
constraints: s consists only of printable ASCII characters.
hints: First strip out anything that isn't a letter or digit, and lowercase everything.
Then compare the cleaned string with its own reverse.

inputs.s: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

title: Reverse String
description: Write a function that reverses a string. The input string is given as `s`. Return the reversed string.
hints: Use two pointers starting at both ends of the string, swapping characters and moving inward.

title: First Unique Character in a String
description: Given a string `s`, find the first non-repeating character in it and return its index. If it does not exist, return `-1`.
constraints: s consists of only lowercase English letters.
hints: Count the frequency of every character first with a hash map.
Scan the string again in order and return the index of the first character whose count is exactly 1.

title: Ransom Note
description: Given two strings `ransomNote` and `magazine`, return `true` if `ransomNote` can be constructed by using the letters from `magazine`, and `false` otherwise. Each letter in `magazine` can only be used once in `ransomNote`.
constraints: ransomNote and magazine consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Count how many of each letter magazine has available.
For ransomNote to be constructible, magazine must have at least as many of each required letter.

title: Longest Common Prefix
description: Write a function to find the longest common prefix string amongst an array of strings `strs`. If there is no common prefix, return an empty string `""`.
hints: The common prefix can never be longer than the shortest string in the array.
Compare characters column by column across all strings until a mismatch or a string ends.

title: Roman to Integer
description: Given a roman numeral string `s`, convert it to an integer. Roman numerals are represented by seven symbols: I (1), V (5), X (10), L (50), C (100), D (500), M (1000), where a smaller value placed before a larger one is subtracted (e.g. IV = 4, IX = 9).
constraints: It is guaranteed that s is a valid roman numeral in the range [1, 3999].
hints: Map each symbol to its value, then scan left to right.
If a symbol's value is smaller than the value right after it, subtract it instead of adding it (this handles cases like IV and IX).

title: Integer to Roman
description: Given an integer `num`, convert it to a roman numeral.
hints: List the roman symbols and their values from largest to smallest, including the subtractive pairs (like 'CM' for 900, 'IV' for 4).
Greedily subtract the largest possible value from num, appending its symbol, until num reaches 0.

title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
description: Given two strings `haystack` and `needle`, return the index of the first occurrence of `needle` in `haystack`, or `-1` if `needle` is not part of `haystack`.
constraints: haystack and needle consist of only lowercase English characters.
hints: Try every possible starting index in haystack where needle could fit.
At each candidate starting index, check whether the substring of that length matches needle exactly.

title: Add Binary
description: Given two binary strings `a` and `b`, return their sum as a binary string.
constraints: a and b consist only of '0' or '1' characters.
Neither a nor b has leading zeros, except for the zero itself.
hints: Add the two binary strings from right to left, just like decimal addition, tracking a carry.
Don't forget to append a final leading '1' if there's a carry left after the last digits.

title: Reverse Words in a String
description: Given an input string `s`, reverse the order of the words. A word is a maximal sequence of non-space characters. Return a string of the words in reverse order, joined by a single space, with no leading, trailing, or multiple spaces between words.
constraints: s contains English letters, digits, and spaces ' '.
There is at least one word in s.
hints: Split the string on whitespace — most languages' split will conveniently drop empty tokens from repeated spaces.
Reverse the resulting list of words and join them with single spaces.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
description: Given a string `s`, return the longest palindromic substring in `s`. If there are multiple substrings of the same maximum length, return the one that starts at the smallest index.
constraints: s consists of digits and English letters.
hints: Every palindrome expands outward from a center, which is either a single character (odd length) or between two characters (even length).
Try expanding around every possible center, scanning left to right, and keep the longest palindrome found (the first one reached in case of a tie).

title: Palindrome Number
description: Given an integer `x`, return `true` if `x` is a palindrome (reads the same forward and backward), and `false` otherwise. Negative numbers are never palindromes.
hints: Negative numbers can never be palindromes because of the leading minus sign.
Convert the number's digits to a string (or reverse them mathematically) and compare front to back.

title: Reverse Integer
description: Given a signed 32-bit integer `x`, return `x` with its digits reversed. If reversing causes the value to go outside the signed 32-bit integer range `[-2^31, 2^31 - 1]`, return `0`.
hints: Handle the sign separately, then reverse the digits of the absolute value.
Check the 32-bit signed range after reversing and return 0 if it overflows.

title: String to Integer (atoi)
description: Implement the `myAtoi(s)` function, which converts a string to a 32-bit signed integer, following these rules: skip leading whitespace, an optional `+`/`-` sign, then digits (stop at the first non-digit). Clamp the result to the signed 32-bit range `[-2^31, 2^31 - 1]`. If no valid conversion is possible, return `0`.
constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, ' ', '+', '-', and '.'.
hints: Process the string step by step: skip whitespace, then read an optional sign, then read consecutive digits.
Stop as soon as you hit a non-digit character, and clamp the final result into the 32-bit signed integer range.

title: Multiply Strings
description: Given two non-negative integers `num1` and `num2` represented as strings, return the product of `num1` and `num2`, also represented as a string. You must not use any built-in big-integer library or convert the inputs directly to integers.
constraints: num1 and num2 consist of digits only.
Neither has leading zeros, except the number 0 itself.
hints: Multiply digit by digit like long multiplication, accumulating results into a result array sized len(num1)+len(num2).
The product of the digits at positions i and j always lands at result positions i+j and i+j+1 — sum those contributions and then handle carries.

title: Decode String
description: Given an encoded string `s` in the form `k[encoded_string]` (meaning the `encoded_string` inside the brackets is repeated exactly `k` times), return its decoded string. `k` is guaranteed to be a positive integer, and the input is always valid, with nested encodings allowed (e.g. `"3[a2[c]]" = "accaccacc"`).
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters, digits, and square brackets '[]'.
s is guaranteed to be a valid encoding.
hints: Use a stack: whenever you see '[', push the current string and repeat count so far; whenever you see ']', pop and repeat.
Numbers can have more than one digit, so accumulate consecutive digit characters before treating them as a single count.

title: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String
description: Given a string `s`, repeatedly remove adjacent duplicate letters (a pair of two identical letters right next to each other) until no adjacent duplicates remain. Return the final string.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: A stack works well: push each character, but if it matches the top of the stack, pop instead.
After processing every character this way, whatever remains on the stack, in order, is the answer.

title: Simplify Path
description: Given an absolute path for a Unix-style file system `path`, convert it to its simplified canonical path. Multiple consecutive slashes are treated as a single slash, `.` refers to the current directory, `..` moves up one directory (ignored at the root), and the canonical path must not end with a trailing slash unless it's the root `/`.
constraints: path is a valid absolute Unix path.
hints: Split the path on '/' and process each segment: ignore empty segments and '.', pop the stack on '..', and push everything else.
Join the remaining stack segments with '/' and prepend a single leading slash.

title: Binary Search
description: Given a sorted (ascending) array of distinct integers `nums` and an integer `target`, write a function to search `target` in `nums`. Return its index if found, otherwise return `-1`. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.
constraints: All the integers in nums are unique, sorted in ascending order.
hints: Keep a low and high pointer bounding the search range.
Compare the target with the middle element each step and halve the search range accordingly.

title: Search Insert Position
description: Given a sorted array of distinct integers `nums` and a target value `target`, return the index if the target is found. If not, return the index where it would be if it were inserted in order. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.
constraints: nums contains distinct values sorted in ascending order.
hints: This is a standard binary search for the leftmost position where target could be inserted.
When the loop ends without finding the target, the low pointer lands exactly on the correct insert position.

title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
description: Given an array of integers `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, find the starting and ending position of a given `target` value. Return `[first, last]`, or `[-1, -1]` if `target` is not found. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.
hints: Run two separate binary searches: one for the leftmost index where target could go, one for the rightmost.
The first search finds the lower bound of target; the second finds the lower bound of target + 1, then steps back one.

title: Find Peak Element
description: A peak element is an element that is strictly greater than its neighbors. Given a 0-indexed integer array `nums`, find a peak element and return its index. If the array contains multiple peaks, return the index of any of them. You may imagine that `nums[-1] = nums[n] = -infinity`. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(log n) time.
constraints: nums[i] != nums[i + 1] for all valid i.
hints: If nums[mid] < nums[mid+1], a peak must exist somewhere to the right (the slope is climbing).
Otherwise, a peak must exist at mid or to its left. Binary search using this rule.

test_cases.explanation: 3 is a peak, and its index 2 is the only valid answer.
2 is a peak, and its index 1 is the only valid answer.

title: Sqrt(x)
description: Given a non-negative integer `x`, return the square root of `x` rounded down to the nearest integer. You must not use any built-in exponent function or operator.
hints: The answer is the largest integer `r` such that `r * r <= x` — binary search for it between 0 and x.

title: Koko Eating Bananas
description: Koko loves bananas. There are `n` piles of bananas, the `i`-th pile has `piles[i]` bananas. Koko can decide her eating speed `k` bananas per hour. Each hour, she chooses one pile and eats `k` bananas from it (if the pile has fewer than `k`, she eats the whole pile and stops that hour). Koko wants to finish all piles within `h` hours. Return the minimum integer `k` such that she can eat all the bananas within `h` hours.
hints: The answer lies somewhere between speed 1 and the size of the largest pile — binary search over that range.
For a candidate speed k, the hours needed is the sum over piles of ceil(pile / k). Find the smallest k where that total is <= h.

title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
description: A conveyor belt has packages `weights[i]` that must be shipped in order, within `days` days. Each day, the ship loads packages (in the given order) up to its weight capacity. Return the least weight capacity that will ship all packages within `days` days.
hints: The capacity must be at least the heaviest single package, and at most the sum of all packages — binary search that range.
For a candidate capacity, greedily simulate loading days: how many days does it take? Find the smallest capacity needing at most the allowed number of days.

title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
description: Given an array of positive integers `nums` and a positive integer `target`, return the minimal length of a contiguous subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to `target`. If there is no such subarray, return `0`.
hints: Since all numbers are positive, a sliding window works: grow the right edge to increase the sum, shrink the left edge whenever the sum is enough.
Track the minimum window length every time the current window's sum meets or exceeds target.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
description: You are given a string `s` and an integer `k`. You can choose any character of the string and change it to any other uppercase English character, at most `k` times. Return the length of the longest substring containing the same letter you can get after performing this many operations.
constraints: s consists of only uppercase English letters.
hints: A window is valid whenever (window length - count of its most frequent character) <= k — that's how many characters would need replacing.
Slide a window across the string, shrinking from the left whenever it becomes invalid, and track the max valid window length.

title: Permutation in String
description: Given two strings `s1` and `s2`, return `true` if `s2` contains a permutation of `s1` as a contiguous substring, or `false` otherwise.
constraints: s1 and s2 consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: A permutation of s1 has the exact same character counts as s1, just reordered — so look for any window of s2 with a matching character-count profile.
Slide a fixed-size window (length of s1) across s2, maintaining a running character count, and compare it to s1's character count.

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
description: Evaluate the value of an arithmetic expression given as an array of tokens `tokens` in Reverse Polish Notation. Valid operators are `+`, `-`, `*`, and `/`. Division between two integers should truncate toward zero. Return the integer result of the expression.
constraints: tokens[i] is either an operator ('+', '-', '*', or '/') or an integer.
hints: Use a stack: push numbers, and whenever you see an operator, pop the top two numbers, apply the operator, and push the result.
Watch the operand order for '-' and '/': the second-popped number comes first.

title: Daily Temperatures
description: Given an array of integers `temperatures` representing daily temperatures, return an array `answer` such that `answer[i]` is the number of days you have to wait after day `i` to get a warmer temperature. If there is no future day for which this is possible, `answer[i] == 0`.
hints: Use a monotonic decreasing stack of indices whose warmer day hasn't been found yet.
When the current temperature is warmer than the temperature at the top of the stack, pop it and record the day difference.

title: Next Greater Element I
description: You are given two distinct 0-indexed integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, where `nums1` is a subset of `nums2`. For each element of `nums1`, find the first element to its right in `nums2` that is greater than it; if none exists, use `-1`. Return an array `ans` of the same length as `nums1`.
constraints: All integers in nums1 and nums2 are unique.
All integers in nums1 also appear in nums2.
hints: Precompute the next-greater-element for every value in nums2 using a monotonic decreasing stack, scanning left to right.
Then just look up each nums1 value in that precomputed map.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
description: Given an array of integers `heights` representing the histogram's bar heights where the width of each bar is 1, return the area of the largest rectangle in the histogram.
hints: For each bar, the largest rectangle using it as the shortest bar extends left and right until a shorter bar is found.
A monotonic increasing stack of indices lets you find, for each bar popped, exactly how far its rectangle extends in O(n) total.

title: Basic Calculator II
description: Given a string `s` representing a non-negative integer arithmetic expression, containing only non-negative integers, `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, and spaces, evaluate it and return the result. Integer division should truncate toward zero. You may assume the given expression is always valid.
constraints: s consists of integers and the characters '+', '-', '*', '/' separated by some spaces.
The expression evaluates to an integer that fits a 32-bit signed range.
hints: '*' and '/' bind tighter than '+' and '-' — resolve them immediately as you scan, pushing the running term onto a stack.
At the end, sum everything on the stack — the '+'/'-' operators just control the sign of each pushed term.

title: Generate Parentheses
description: Given `n` pairs of parentheses, return all combinations of well-formed parentheses strings that can be formed using exactly `n` pairs.
hints: Build the string left to right, tracking how many open and close brackets have been used so far.
You can add an open bracket whenever you've used fewer than n, and a close bracket only when it wouldn't outnumber the open brackets so far.

title: Number of Islands
description: Given an `m x n` 2D binary grid `grid` which represents a map of `'1'`s (land) and `'0'`s (water), return the number of islands. An island is surrounded by water and is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically. Each row of the grid is given as a string of `'0'`/`'1'` characters.
hints: Scan every cell; whenever you find an unvisited '1', that's a brand-new island.
From that cell, flood-fill (BFS or DFS) through all connected '1's, marking them visited, then increment the island count.

title: Max Area of Island
description: You are given an `m x n` binary matrix `grid` where `1` represents land and `0` represents water. An island is a group of `1`s connected 4-directionally. Return the maximum area of an island in `grid` (or `0` if there is no island).
hints: Same flood-fill idea as counting islands, but have each flood-fill return the number of cells it visited.
Track the maximum area returned across every unvisited land cell you start a flood-fill from.

title: Flood Fill
description: You are given an `image` represented by an `m x n` grid of integers, and three integers `sr`, `sc`, and `color`. Perform a flood fill starting from pixel `(sr, sc)`: change the color of the starting pixel and every pixel connected 4-directionally with the same original color to `color`. Return the modified image.
hints: If the new color is the same as the starting pixel's color, there's nothing to do (and you must avoid infinite recursion in that case).
DFS/BFS from (sr, sc), recoloring every 4-directionally connected pixel that still has the original color.

title: Rotting Oranges
description: You are given an `m x n` grid where each cell can be `0` (empty), `1` (fresh orange), or `2` (rotten orange). Every minute, any fresh orange 4-directionally adjacent to a rotten orange becomes rotten. Return the minimum number of minutes until no cell has a fresh orange, or `-1` if that is impossible.
hints: This is multi-source BFS: start with every initially rotten orange in the queue at once, at minute 0.
Each BFS layer represents one minute passing; if fresh oranges remain after BFS finishes, return -1.

title: Course Schedule
description: There are `numCourses` courses labeled `0` to `numCourses - 1`. You are given `prerequisites` where `prerequisites[i] = [a, b]` means you must take course `b` before course `a`. Return `true` if you can finish all courses (i.e., there is no cycle in the prerequisite graph), otherwise `false`.
hints: This is a cycle-detection problem on a directed graph.
Do a topological sort (Kahn's algorithm using in-degrees): if you can process all numCourses nodes, there's no cycle.

title: Course Schedule II
description: There are `numCourses` courses labeled `0` to `numCourses - 1`. You are given `prerequisites` where `prerequisites[i] = [a, b]` means you must take course `b` before course `a`. Return a valid ordering of courses to finish all of them, always preferring the course with the smallest label among those currently available to take. If it is impossible to finish all courses, return an empty array.
hints: Use Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take an available course (in-degree 0) and remove it, updating in-degrees of its dependents.
To get a deterministic answer, always pick the smallest-labeled course among those currently available — a min-heap works well for this.

title: Number of Provinces
description: There are `n` cities. `isConnected[i][j] = 1` if city `i` and city `j` are directly connected, and `0` otherwise. A province is a group of directly or indirectly connected cities. Return the total number of provinces.
hints: This is a connected-components problem — the adjacency matrix defines an undirected graph.
Union-Find (or a simple DFS/BFS from every unvisited city) counts how many separate components exist.

title: Word Ladder
description: Given two words `beginWord` and `endWord`, and a dictionary `wordList`, return the number of words in the shortest transformation sequence from `beginWord` to `endWord` (inclusive of both endpoints), changing only one letter at a time, with every intermediate word required to exist in `wordList`. Return `0` if no such sequence exists.
constraints: All words have the same length and consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Treat each word as a node; an edge connects two words that differ by exactly one letter.
BFS from beginWord finds the shortest path length in an unweighted graph — for each word, try changing every position to every other letter to find neighbors present in wordList.

title: Is Graph Bipartite?
description: There is an undirected graph with `n` nodes, where each node is labeled from `0` to `n - 1`. You are given `graph` where `graph[u]` is a list of nodes adjacent to node `u`. Return `true` if the graph is bipartite (its nodes can be split into two independent sets such that every edge connects a node in one set to a node in the other).
constraints: graph[u] does not contain u, and has no duplicate values.
hints: Try to 2-color the graph: color each node's neighbors the opposite color of itself.
If you ever need to color a node that's already colored the same as its neighbor, the graph is not bipartite. Remember to check every connected component.

title: Network Delay Time
description: You are given a network of `n` nodes labeled `1` to `n`. `times[i] = [ui, vi, wi]` represents a directed edge from node `ui` to node `vi` with travel time `wi`. Starting from node `k`, return the minimum time it takes for a signal to reach all `n` nodes. If it is impossible, return `-1`.
hints: This is a single-source shortest path problem on a weighted directed graph — Dijkstra's algorithm fits perfectly.
The answer is the maximum shortest-path distance from k to any node; if any node is unreachable, return -1.

title: Redundant Connection
description: You are given a graph that started as a tree with `n` nodes labeled `1` to `n`, with one additional edge added, creating exactly one cycle. `edges[i] = [ai, bi]` indicates an edge between nodes `ai` and `bi`. Return the edge that, if removed, results in a tree. If multiple answers exist, return the one that occurs last in the input.
hints: Process edges in order, using Union-Find to merge the two endpoints of each edge.
The first edge whose two endpoints are already in the same component is the redundant one — return it immediately.

title: Rotate Image
description: You are given an `n x n` 2D matrix representing an image. Rotate the image by 90 degrees clockwise and return the rotated matrix.
hints: A 90-degree clockwise rotation is the same as transposing the matrix and then reversing each row.

title: Spiral Matrix
description: Given an `m x n` matrix, return all elements of the matrix in spiral order (starting at the top-left, moving right, then down, then left, then up, and so on inward).
hints: Maintain four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) and peel off one layer of the matrix at a time.
After traversing the top row, right column, bottom row, and left column of the current layer, shrink the boundaries inward and repeat.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
description: Given an `m x n` integer matrix, if an element is `0`, set its entire row and column to `0`. Return the modified matrix.
hints: First scan the whole matrix and record which rows and which columns contain at least one zero.
Then make a second pass, zeroing out every cell whose row or column was marked.

title: Search a 2D Matrix
description: You are given an `m x n` integer matrix `matrix` with the following properties: each row is sorted in non-decreasing order, and the first integer of each row is greater than the last integer of the previous row. Given an integer `target`, return `true` if `target` is in `matrix`, or `false` otherwise. You must write a solution in O(log(m * n)) time.
hints: Because of how the matrix is structured, you can treat it as one giant sorted array of length m*n.
Binary search over indices 0..m*n-1, converting each mid index to a (row, col) pair via division and modulo.

title: Game of Life
description: According to Conway's Game of Life, given an `m x n` grid `board` where each cell is `1` (live) or `0` (dead), compute the next state of the board: any live cell with fewer than two or more than three live neighbors dies, any live cell with two or three live neighbors survives, and any dead cell with exactly three live neighbors becomes alive. Return the next state.
hints: For each cell, count its live neighbors among all 8 surrounding cells using the original board state.
Apply the four rules to build a brand-new board so that updates to one cell don't affect the neighbor count of cells processed later.

title: Valid Sudoku
description: Determine if a `9 x 9` Sudoku board is valid: each row, column, and each of the nine `3x3` sub-boxes must contain the digits `1-9` without repetition. Empty cells are represented by `0` and are ignored. Only the filled cells need to be validated according to the rules; the board does not need to be fully solvable.
hints: Track seen digits separately for each of the 9 rows, 9 columns, and 9 sub-boxes.
For each filled cell, compute its sub-box index as (row/3)*3 + col/3, and check/record it against all three tracking sets.

test_cases.explanation: This is a valid Sudoku layout.
Two 8s appear in the top-left 3x3 sub-box, so it is invalid.
Two 5s appear in the first row, so it is invalid.

title: Insert Interval
description: You are given an array of non-overlapping intervals `intervals` sorted by start time, and a new interval `newInterval`. Insert `newInterval` into `intervals`, merging any overlapping intervals, and return the resulting array still sorted by start time.
constraints: intervals is sorted by starti in ascending order.
hints: First append every interval that ends strictly before newInterval starts, unchanged.
Then merge every interval that overlaps newInterval into it (expanding its bounds), and finally append the rest unchanged.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
description: Given an array of intervals `intervals`, return the minimum number of intervals you need to remove to make the rest of the intervals non-overlapping (intervals that only touch at an endpoint are not considered overlapping).
hints: Sort the intervals by end time — a greedy strategy that always keeps the interval that ends earliest leaves the most room for future intervals.
Walk through sorted intervals, keeping track of the end of the last kept interval; any interval that starts before that end must be removed.

title: Meeting Rooms II
description: Given an array of meeting time intervals `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [starti, endi]`, return the minimum number of conference rooms required to hold all the meetings.
hints: Separate and sort all start times and all end times independently.
Walk through sorted start times with a pointer into sorted end times: a new room is needed whenever the next meeting starts before the earliest currently-running meeting ends.

title: Task Scheduler
description: You are given an array of CPU `tasks`, each represented by an uppercase letter, and an integer `n`. Each task takes one unit of time, and identical tasks must be separated by at least `n` units of time (the CPU may be idle during that gap). Return the minimum number of time units the CPU needs to finish all tasks.
constraints: tasks[i] is an uppercase English letter.
hints: The most frequent task determines the overall structure — it needs (maxFreq - 1) gaps of size (n + 1) after it.
The answer is the larger of: the total task count, or (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + (number of tasks tied for the max frequency).

title: Partition Labels
description: You are given a string `s`. Partition it into as many parts as possible so that each letter appears in at most one part, and return an array of integers representing the size of each part (the parts must, when concatenated in order, reproduce `s`).
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: For each character, precompute the last index at which it appears in the string.
Scan left to right, extending the current partition's end to the max last-occurrence seen so far; when the current index reaches that end, close the partition.

title: Climbing Stairs
description: You are climbing a staircase that takes `n` steps to reach the top. Each time you can climb either 1 or 2 steps. Return the number of distinct ways you can climb to the top.
hints: The number of ways to reach step n is the number of ways to reach step n-1 plus the number of ways to reach step n-2 (your last move was either a 1-step or a 2-step).
This is just the Fibonacci sequence in disguise.

title: House Robber
description: You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street, represented by an array `nums` where `nums[i]` is the amount of money in house `i`. Adjacent houses have connected security systems, so you cannot rob two adjacent houses on the same night. Return the maximum amount of money you can rob without alerting the police.
hints: At each house, you either skip it (keeping the best total so far) or rob it (best total from two houses back, plus this house's value).
Track two running values: the best total up to the previous house, and the best total up to the house before that.

title: House Robber II
description: This is a variant of House Robber where the houses (`nums`) are arranged in a circle — the first and last house are adjacent. You still cannot rob two adjacent houses. Return the maximum amount of money you can rob.
hints: Since the first and last houses can't both be robbed, the answer is the better of two linear House Robber runs: one excluding the first house, one excluding the last house.

title: Coin Change
description: You are given an integer array `coins` representing coin denominations and an integer `amount`. Return the fewest number of coins needed to make up `amount`. If that amount cannot be made up by any combination of the coins, return `-1`. You may assume an unlimited supply of each coin.
hints: Build up the answer bottom-up: dp[x] = minimum coins to make amount x, with dp[0] = 0.
For each amount from 1 to the target, try every coin and take dp[x] = min(dp[x], dp[x - coin] + 1) whenever x - coin is reachable.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
hints: dp[i] can represent the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending exactly at index i.
For a faster O(n log n) approach, maintain a list of the smallest possible tail value for every achievable subsequence length, using binary search to update it.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
description: Given two strings `text1` and `text2`, return the length of their longest common subsequence (a sequence that appears in both strings in the same relative order, not necessarily contiguous). Return `0` if there is no common subsequence.
constraints: text1 and text2 consist of lowercase English characters.
hints: Build a 2D table dp[i][j] = LCS length of text1[:i] and text2[:j].
If the characters at position i-1 and j-1 match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).

title: Edit Distance
description: Given two strings `word1` and `word2`, return the minimum number of single-character operations (insert, delete, or replace) required to convert `word1` into `word2`.
constraints: word1 and word2 consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Build dp[i][j] = edit distance between the first i characters of word1 and first j characters of word2.
If the current characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise it's 1 + the minimum of the insert/delete/replace neighbors.

title: Word Break
description: Given a string `s` and a dictionary of strings `wordDict`, return `true` if `s` can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words. The same word may be reused multiple times.
constraints: s and wordDict[i] consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Let dp[i] mean 's[:i]' can be segmented using dictionary words; dp[0] = true.
dp[i] is true if there's some earlier true dp[j] such that s[j:i] is a word in the dictionary.

title: Unique Paths
description: A robot is located at the top-left corner of an `m x n` grid. It can only move either down or right at any point in time, trying to reach the bottom-right corner. Return the number of possible unique paths.
hints: The number of ways to reach a cell is the sum of the ways to reach the cell above it and the cell to its left.
The first row and first column each only have exactly one way to reach every cell in them (always moving in a straight line).

title: Minimum Path Sum
description: Given an `m x n` grid filled with non-negative numbers, find a path from top-left to bottom-right which minimizes the sum of all numbers along its path. You can only move either down or right at any point in time.
hints: The minimum cost to reach a cell is its own value plus the smaller of the minimum cost to reach the cell above or the cell to its left.
The first row and first column can only be reached one way each, so fill them in first.

title: Jump Game
description: You are given an integer array `nums`. You are initially positioned at the first index, and each element represents your maximum jump length at that position. Return `true` if you can reach the last index, or `false` otherwise.
hints: Track the farthest index reachable so far as you scan left to right.
If you ever reach an index beyond the farthest reachable point, you're stuck — otherwise, keep extending the farthest reach with i + nums[i].

title: Jump Game II
description: You are given a 0-indexed array of integers `nums` of length `n`, starting at index 0, where each element represents your maximum jump length. Return the minimum number of jumps to reach index `n - 1`. It is guaranteed that you can always reach the last index.
constraints: It is guaranteed that you can reach nums[n - 1].
hints: Think in terms of 'jump levels': all the positions reachable using exactly k jumps form a contiguous range.
Greedily track the current jump's boundary and the farthest reachable point; increment the jump count whenever you cross the current boundary.

title: Decode Ways
description: A message containing letters A-Z is encoded using the mapping 'A' -> 1, 'B' -> 2, ..., 'Z' -> 26. Given a string `s` containing only digits, return the number of ways to decode it.
constraints: s contains only digits and may contain leading zero(s).
hints: dp[i] = number of ways to decode the first i characters of s; a '0' can never stand alone as a valid single-digit code.
dp[i] adds dp[i-1] if s[i-1] is a valid 1-digit code (1-9), and adds dp[i-2] if s[i-2:i] is a valid 2-digit code (10-26).

title: Subsets
description: Given an integer array `nums` of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set). The solution set must not contain duplicate subsets.
constraints: All the numbers of nums are unique.
hints: Every subset can be described by, for each element, a binary choice: include it or not.
Backtrack through the array, at each index branching into 'include nums[i]' and 'exclude nums[i]', adding the current partial subset to the result at every step.

title: Permutations
description: Given an array `nums` of distinct integers, return all the possible permutations of the array, in any order.
constraints: All integers of nums are unique.
hints: Backtrack by building a partial permutation and tracking which numbers have already been used.
At each step, try every not-yet-used number as the next element, recurse, then undo the choice before trying the next one.

title: Combination Sum
description: Given an array of distinct integers `candidates` and a target integer `target`, return a list of all unique combinations of `candidates` where the chosen numbers sum to `target`. The same number may be chosen from `candidates` an unlimited number of times. Each combination should be listed with its values in ascending order.
constraints: All elements of candidates are distinct.
hints: Sort the candidates first, then backtrack: at each step, either reuse the current candidate again or move on to the next one.
Since the same number can repeat, when you choose candidates[i], recurse while still allowing index i again (not i+1) — but stop early once the running sum exceeds target.

title: Word Search
description: Given an `m x n` grid of characters `board` (each row given as a string) and a string `word`, return `true` if `word` exists in the grid, formed by sequentially adjacent cells (horizontally or vertically neighboring), where the same cell may not be used more than once.
hints: Try starting the search from every cell that matches the word's first letter.
DFS/backtrack character by character into unvisited neighboring cells, marking cells as visited temporarily and un-marking them when backtracking.

title: N-Queens II
description: The n-queens puzzle is the problem of placing `n` queens on an `n x n` chessboard such that no two queens attack each other (no shared row, column, or diagonal). Given an integer `n`, return the number of distinct solutions to the n-queens puzzle.
hints: Place queens one row at a time — since no two queens can share a row, this guarantees no row conflicts automatically.
Track which columns and which diagonals (row - col, and row + col) are already occupied to check placements in O(1).

title: Counting Bits
description: Given an integer `n`, return an array `ans` of length `n + 1` such that for each `i` (0 <= i <= n), `ans[i]` is the number of `1`'s in the binary representation of `i`.
hints: Every number i can be related to a smaller, already-computed number: i >> 1 (i with its lowest bit dropped).
ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1) — the popcount of i equals the popcount of i without its last bit, plus that last bit itself.
